subject: Fitting coupled ODE a'la Kuramoto model

messages.author: 3fe7cb4df4d836ab
messages.subject: Fitting coupled ODE a'la Kuramoto model
parts:
Could someone help/direct me in building Stan model for a coupled ODE? I'm going through documentation, but it's quite a big document. There seems to be an example of coupled ODE (Fig. 19.3, p. 260), but in order to modify it probably should first understand a bit of it. I already have model coded in Python using emcce hammer, but heard that NUTS is magic making technique that everyone should use for everything.

The model in first approximation can be thought of as Kuramoto, where changes in phases depend on pairwise differences phase differences:
d ϕ_{i} / d t = w_{i} + sum_{all osc} k_{i j} sin( ϕ_{j} - ϕ_{i} )

In second step, these phases are additionally transformed and only then compared to measurements, i.e. I'm minimising for
LSE = Least_Mean_Square( Input_Signal, Reconstructed_Signal ),
where Reconstructed_Signal = sum_i ( important_function( ϕ_i, A_i )

Now I would like to determine parameters for Kuramoto-like model and these scaling A_i factors. I have a priories for these parameters (initially assume normals or uniform) and measured phases to which model should be fitted.

I'll continue reading and hopefully will provide soon with some initial version. Any feedback/help is extremely welcomed.

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: Fitting coupled ODE a'la Kuramoto model
parts:
Hi!

Ähm... how many of those coupled oscillators do you have? What you want to do sounds possible to me to do in Stan, it's just that ODEs are computationally very expensive such that the number of Oscillators may better be small otherwise things will be very slow.

On my problems which I solve with the Stan ODE solver I endup having to calculate the solution to the ODE system between 10^5 to 10^6 solves per MCMC chain.

Sebastian

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: Fitting coupled ODE a'la Kuramoto model
parts:
Oha... if you mean you want to put S=100 ODE equations into Stan, then this is the largest I have ever seen. Note that Stan must calculate the sensitivities of the ODEs. That means it calculates for all S states the derivatives wrt to all parameters. You end up with having to solve S * (1 + P) ODE equations if P is the total number of parameters and here I assume that your initial condition is known.

If this works then this would be so cool, but it will be hard and as a start you maybe should not start with full Bayes but rather optimization or ADVI.

Your problem would indeed benefit from putting it onto a GPU which is doable. Assuming you can live with the non-stiff solver which uses odeint, then it should be doable with reasonable effort to put this on a GPU. Boosts odeint has bindings to various GPU frameworks which should make it doable.

Sebastian

PS: I do not know these problems, but a FFT is in the works and maybe this helps you to reformulate the problem?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting coupled ODE a'la Kuramoto model
parts:
I'd just code it up and then see how well it scales with
multiple ODEs. We've run large numbers of ODEs as parts of
likelihood calculations, but not ones with huge numbers of
parameters because internally we wind up needing Jacobians for
stiff systems and even for non-stiff systems we need the
derivatives of all state solutions w.r.t. parameters. This
lets us solve the ODEs with control on the sensitivity (derivative)
errors.

In Bayesian models, we don't think in terms of things like least
squares algorithms. Instead, we'd build a forward model of the
scientific process that depends on some unknown parameters about
which we'd like to learn (this may be deterministic and have unexplained
errors), and couple that with a model of the measurement process (such
as taking a stopwatch and ruler to measure a pendulum). Then we
just run standard Bayesian inference to calculate probabilities over
the parameters conditioned on the data (so-called Bayesian inversion).

You could run Stan's maximum likelihood inference, which just
chooses optimal parameters. If the noise is Gaussian, this
reduces to least squares.

- Bob
